headwords.definition: a person's parents, children, siblings, or partner
examples: My immediate family lives in three different cities.
We usually reserve the first evening of the holiday for immediate family.

headwords.definition: relatives beyond parents, children, siblings, and partners
examples: Our extended family gathers at my aunt's home each spring.
Living near extended family made emergency childcare easier.

headwords.definition: a person connected to someone by family
examples: A distant relative recognized me from an old family photograph.
Several relatives helped prepare food for the celebration.

headwords.definition: a brother or sister
examples: My older sibling taught me how to travel by bus alone.
The siblings divided responsibility for their father's appointments.

headwords.definition: a person who has no brothers or sisters
examples: As an only child, she spent a great deal of time with cousins.
Being an only child does not necessarily mean growing up lonely.
collocations: grow up as an only child

headwords.definition: the people who live together in one home
examples: Everyone in the household contributes to the grocery list.
The household includes two generations and a university student.

headwords.definition: a household or family unit centered on parents and their children
examples: The television show presented the nuclear family as the only normal arrangement.
A nuclear family may still rely heavily on grandparents and cousins.

headwords.definition: involving one parent raising one or more children
examples: The school changed meeting times after listening to single-parent families.
A single-parent household may need especially reliable childcare.

headwords.definition: a family in which partners bring children from earlier relationships
examples: The blended family created new holiday routines that included everyone.
Patience helped the children adjust to life in a blended family.

headwords.definition: having strong, supportive relationships among members
examples: She grew up in a close-knit family where cousins met every week.
A close-knit household can still respect individual privacy.

headwords.definition: a strong emotional connection between people
examples: Cooking together strengthened the bond between the grandfather and child.
Distance did not weaken their sibling bond because they called regularly.

headwords.definition: the feeling of being accepted and included in a group
examples: Shared routines gave the adopted child a growing sense of belonging.
Family belonging should not depend on agreeing about every decision.

phrases.text: Families can take many different forms.
We remain close even though we do not live nearby.
The relationship has changed as we have grown older.
Extended family provides a wider support network.
Living together does not automatically create emotional closeness.
phrases.reusable_core: does not automatically create emotional closeness

phrases.text: We make an effort to stay in regular contact.
The household includes people at different stages of life.
A strong bond can survive periods of disagreement.
The arrangement works because everyone has some privacy.
Family membership is based on care as well as biology.
I feel accepted without having to hide important parts of myself.
No single structure suits every family.

headwords.definition: practical, emotional, or financial help given to someone
examples: Family support helped her continue studying after the baby was born.
He wanted emotional support rather than immediate advice.

headwords.definition: to help someone emotionally, practically, or financially
examples: My parents supported my decision even though it worried them.
The siblings support their grandmother by sharing weekly visits.

headwords.definition: to give someone confidence or motivation
examples: My uncle encouraged me to apply for the course.
Parents can encourage effort without demanding perfect results.

headwords.definition: to make someone feel less worried or uncertain
examples: Her sister reassured her before the medical appointment.
A familiar bedtime routine reassures a young child after a move.

headwords.definition: an opinion or suggestion about what someone should do
examples: I ask my older cousin for career advice because she knows the field.
Unrequested advice can feel like criticism during a stressful moment.

headwords.definition: to recommend a course of action
examples: My father advised me to read the contract before signing.
I would not advise a relative to make a decision I did not understand.

headwords.definition: to depend on someone or something for help
examples: We rely on our neighbor as well as relatives for emergencies.
Adult children should not be expected to rely on parents forever.

headwords.definition: confidence that someone is honest, reliable, or caring
examples: Trust returned slowly after the family discussed what had happened.
Children need trust as they begin making choices alone.

headwords.definition: to share private thoughts or worries with someone trusted
examples: I confide in my sister because she listens before offering solutions.
The teenager found it easier to confide in an aunt than a parent.

headwords.definition: the ability to understand another person's feelings or situation
examples: Empathy helped the parents recognize why the move upset their child.
Different generations need empathy when their pressures are unfamiliar to one another.

headwords.definition: reliably available and responsible
examples: My brother is dependable when someone needs transport to an appointment.
Children feel secure when adults are calm and dependable.

phrases.text: Sometimes people need to be heard before they need advice.
I can depend on them in a genuine emergency.
Support should not become control.
The advice comes from experience, but the final choice is mine.
We help one another in different ways.
A calm conversation can make a difficult situation feel manageable.
Trust develops through small reliable actions.
I would ask what kind of help the person actually wants.
Family support can reduce isolation during a crisis.
Being dependable matters more than making dramatic promises.
Emotional closeness needs privacy as well as honesty.

headwords.definition: a regular pattern of activities
examples: Our evening routine includes preparing lunch for the next day.
A stable routine helped the children adjust after moving.

headwords.definition: a meal eaten together by members of a family or household
examples: Sunday lunch is the only family meal everyone can attend.
The family meal became stressful when phones were constantly checked.

headwords.definition: a routine household task
examples: Each child chooses one daily chore and one weekend task.
Washing dishes feels less like a chore when people talk while doing it.

headwords.definition: work involved in cleaning and managing a home
examples: Paid work does not remove the need to divide housework fairly.
The family completed the housework before guests arrived.

headwords.definition: a duty someone is expected to handle
examples: Checking on the elderly relative is a shared family responsibility.
The teenager gained responsibility by managing her own laundry.

headwords.definition: to separate work or duties among people
examples: We divide household tasks according to time and ability.
The siblings divided the holiday preparations rather than leaving everything to one person.

headwords.definition: to give time, effort, money, or ideas to a shared purpose
examples: Everyone contributes to the household in a way they can manage.
The children contributed by setting the table and feeding the pet.

headwords.definition: a reasonable portion of work or responsibility
examples: Each adult should do a fair share of unpaid household work.
Her fair share changed temporarily while she recovered from surgery.

headwords.definition: paid or unpaid work involved in looking after children, older people, or others
examples: Care work is often invisible until the usual caregiver becomes ill.
The household counted care work when dividing other chores.

headwords.definition: a plan showing when activities or duties happen
examples: A shared schedule prevents two people from assuming the other will collect the child.
The meal schedule became more flexible as the teenagers grew older.

phrases.text: We divide chores according to time and ability.
The routine gives the day a predictable shape.
Eating together creates a natural time to talk.
Household work should not automatically fall to one person.
Everyone contributes in a way that matches their age.
The arrangement needs to change when someone's workload changes.
Care work deserves to be recognized as real work.
A shared calendar reduces last-minute confusion.
The goal is a fair contribution, not identical tasks.
Routine can create security without becoming rigid.

headwords.definition: to share information, feelings, or needs
examples: We communicate more clearly when difficult topics are not raised during an argument.
The parents communicated the new rule and explained its reason.

headwords.definition: a failure to understand someone correctly
examples: A text message caused a misunderstanding about the meeting time.
The misunderstanding ended when each person explained what they had assumed.

headwords.definition: a situation in which people have different opinions
examples: The family disagreement concerned money, not affection.
They handled the disagreement privately instead of involving every relative.

headwords.definition: a serious or continuing disagreement
examples: Unclear caregiving duties created conflict among the siblings.
Avoiding every conflict allowed resentment to grow.

headwords.definition: an agreement in which each side accepts less than originally wanted
examples: The holiday plan was a compromise between two family traditions.
A fair compromise let the teenager attend the event and return at an agreed time.

headwords.definition: a limit that protects privacy, time, or acceptable treatment
examples: Turning off the phone during work is one boundary with relatives.
The parents respected the adult child's boundary about unannounced visits.

headwords.definition: to become involved in a situation where involvement is unwanted or unhelpful
examples: Relatives should not interfere in every parenting decision.
Her brother meant to help but interfered before understanding the problem.

headwords.definition: showing consideration for another person's dignity and rights
examples: A respectful disagreement avoids insults and threats.
The child can question a rule in a respectful way.

headwords.definition: to express regret for something wrong or hurtful
examples: He apologized for sharing the private news without permission.
Parents should apologize when they judge a child unfairly.

headwords.definition: to stop holding anger against someone for a wrong
examples: She forgave the mistake after seeing genuine change.
Forgiving a relative does not require accepting the same harmful behavior again.

phrases.text: I would raise the issue when everyone is calm.
We can disagree without treating the relationship as a competition.
The problem came from different assumptions.
A boundary protects the relationship as well as the individual.
I would explain the effect of the behavior rather than attack the person.
A sincere apology includes a change in behavior.
Compromise is useful when both needs are legitimate.
Privacy should not be interpreted as rejection.
Unresolved resentment can return during an unrelated argument.
Respect is shown through listening, not only polite words.

sections.title: Parents, Children, and Raising a Family

headwords.definition: the activity and approach of raising children
examples: Parenting changes as a child becomes more independent.
The couple discussed parenting expectations before having children.

headwords.definition: to care for and guide a child as they grow
examples: Her grandparents helped raise her while her mother worked abroad.
Parents can raise confident children without removing every difficulty.

headwords.definition: the way a child is cared for and taught while growing up
examples: His upbringing emphasized hospitality and responsibility.
Two siblings can respond differently to the same upbringing.

headwords.definition: methods used to teach children rules and self-control
examples: Effective discipline explains consequences rather than relying on fear.
The parents disagreed about discipline but discussed it away from the child.

headwords.definition: a stated expectation about permitted behavior
examples: The family rule requires everyone to message if they will be late.
A rule becomes easier to follow when its purpose is clear.

headwords.definition: a result of an action, especially one used to teach responsibility
examples: The consequence for missing chores was losing some weekend screen time.
Natural consequences can teach more than an unrelated punishment.

headwords.definition: wanting to keep someone safe from harm
examples: Her parents were protective after the accident but gradually restored her freedom.
Being protective should not prevent teenagers from learning ordinary independence.

headwords.definition: the ability and freedom to make decisions and act without constant help
examples: Managing a small allowance taught the child financial independence.
Teenagers need increasing independence alongside clear safety expectations.

headwords.definition: a person whose behavior provides an example for others
examples: Children notice how adult role models handle mistakes.
An older cousin became a role model without trying to replace the parents.

headwords.definition: time spent giving full, meaningful attention to a relationship
examples: A short walk can be better quality time than an evening of distracted television.
The parent protected some quality time despite a busy work schedule.

phrases.text: Children need age-appropriate freedom and responsibility.
A rule is easier to accept when its purpose is explained.
Parents teach through their behavior as well as their words.
Protection should gradually make room for independence.
The consequence should be related to the behavior.
Consistency matters, but circumstances still need judgment.
Quality time requires attention rather than expensive activities.
Children can contribute to decisions that affect them.
Different children may need different kinds of support.

headwords.definition: people born during a similar period, or one level in a family
examples: Three generations attended the family celebration.
Each generation experienced different technology during adolescence.

headwords.definition: differences in experience, values, or communication between age groups
examples: Smartphone rules became one sign of the generation gap.
Shared work reduced the generation gap between them.

headwords.definition: an older person, especially one respected in a family or community
examples: A family elder explained the history behind the ceremony.
Respecting elders includes listening to their wishes about care.

headwords.definition: unfair treatment or assumptions based on age
examples: Ageism can make employers ignore both older and very young applicants.
The advertisement presented every older adult as helpless, which was ageist.

headwords.definition: good judgment developed through knowledge and experience
examples: Her grandmother's wisdom came from asking practical questions.
Age can bring wisdom, but older people can also make mistakes.

headwords.definition: no longer useful because circumstances have changed
examples: The career advice was outdated in a digital job market.
An old tradition is not automatically outdated if it still has meaning.

headwords.definition: willing to consider unfamiliar ideas without immediate rejection
examples: The grandfather was open-minded about his granddaughter's career choice.
Young people also need to remain open-minded about older experience.

headwords.definition: involving or connecting different generations
examples: The intergenerational project paired teenagers with older storytellers.
Intergenerational housing can reduce loneliness and living costs.

headwords.definition: to guide a less experienced or younger person
examples: A retired engineer mentors students at the community center.
Older siblings often mentor younger ones informally.

headwords.definition: a way of understanding something shaped by experience
examples: Her parents' perspective on job security came from an earlier crisis.
Family discussions improve when each generation explains its perspective.

phrases.text: Different experiences shape what each generation considers normal.
Age does not guarantee wisdom or prevent learning.
Older relatives can offer history that is not written down.
phrases.reusable_core: history that is not written down

phrases.text: Young people can help family members use new tools without embarrassment.
Respect needs to work in both directions.
The advice made sense in a different economic situation.
Shared activities create conversation more naturally than formal lectures.
We can preserve a tradition while changing one part of it.
A generation gap becomes smaller when people explain their reasons.
Each age group has knowledge the other may lack.

sections.title: Living With Family and Living Independently

headwords.definition: able to manage life and decisions without relying heavily on others
examples: Living alone made her more independent in practical matters.
An independent adult can still ask family for emotional support.

headwords.definition: to leave a shared family home and live elsewhere
examples: He moved out when he found work near the city center.
High rent made it difficult for the couple to move out.

headwords.definition: to return to a former family home
examples: She moved back temporarily after losing her job.
Moving back gave him time to retrain without expensive debt.

headwords.definition: freedom from unwanted observation or interruption
examples: The teenager needed privacy to talk with a friend.
People sharing a small home can still protect privacy through routines.

headwords.definition: physical or emotional room belonging to an individual
examples: A curtain created some personal space in the shared bedroom.
Even close relatives need personal space after a stressful day.

headwords.definition: a person who shares a home or room
examples: Living with a roommate reduced costs and taught negotiation.
The roommate agreement covered cleaning, guests, and bills.

headwords.definition: able to provide for and manage oneself without regular help
examples: Cooking and budgeting helped the student become self-sufficient.
No one is completely self-sufficient during every stage of life.

headwords.definition: sad because of being away from home or familiar people
examples: She felt homesick during the first quiet weekend at university.
Regular calls helped without preventing him from building a new life.

headwords.definition: to live together in the same home
examples: Three adult generations cohabit because housing costs are high.
Families cohabit successfully when money and privacy are discussed.

headwords.definition: money, work, or care given to support a shared home
examples: The adult son made a household contribution through rent and cooking.
A contribution should reflect income as well as use of the home.

phrases.text: Living independently teaches practical responsibility.
Staying with family can be a sensible financial choice.
Adult family members need clear expectations about money and chores.
Independence does not mean refusing every kind of help.
Limited space makes privacy harder but still important.
Moving back can be a temporary strategy rather than a failure.
The arrangement allows people to share both costs and care.
I would agree on guests and quiet hours in advance.
The right time to leave depends partly on housing and income.
phrases.reusable_core: depends partly on housing and income

headwords.definition: a custom passed through a family or community
examples: Our family tradition is to cook together before the new year.
The tradition changed when several relatives moved abroad.

headwords.definition: an established way of behaving in a family or culture
examples: Guests learn the household custom of removing shoes.
The wedding combined customs from both families.

headwords.definition: an event marking a happy or important occasion
examples: The graduation celebration was small but meaningful.
Video calls allowed distant relatives to join the celebration.

headwords.definition: a repeated meaningful action connected to an event or routine
examples: Reading the same story became a bedtime ritual.
The holiday ritual gives children something familiar to expect.

headwords.definition: traditions, stories, and culture inherited from earlier generations
examples: Recipes are an important part of her family heritage.
The archive helps younger relatives explore their heritage.

headwords.definition: a principle considered important in guiding behavior
examples: Hospitality is a family value learned through practice.
Relatives may share values while expressing them differently.

headwords.definition: to give knowledge or traditions to a younger generation
examples: Her grandfather passed down the recipe by cooking beside her.
Families pass stories down even when details change.

headwords.definition: to keep something important from disappearing
examples: Recording the elder's stories helped preserve family history.
A tradition is easier to preserve when young people participate.

headwords.definition: to change something so it works in new circumstances
examples: We adapted the celebration so relatives could join online.
Families adapt routines when children become adults.

phrases.text: The tradition creates continuity across generations.
A celebration can be meaningful without being expensive.
Young people should understand the reason behind the custom.
Traditions survive when they can adapt.
The family keeps the central meaning while changing the format.
Stories and recipes carry history in an everyday form.
No one should be forced to follow a harmful tradition.
Shared values do not require identical lifestyles.
New family members can contribute their own customs.

sections.title: Caregiving, Older Relatives, and Family Change

headwords.definition: a person who regularly looks after someone needing help
examples: The main caregiver needed one afternoon each week for rest.
Several relatives shared care instead of relying on one daughter.

headwords.definition: the work of looking after a child, older adult, or ill person
examples: Caregiving affected her work schedule and sleep.
The siblings made a written caregiving plan.

headwords.definition: a person who relies on someone for financial or practical support
examples: The insurance plan covers two child dependents.
An older dependent may need transport but still make decisions.

headwords.definition: physically weak and easily harmed
examples: The frail grandfather needed a handrail but not constant supervision.
Calling every older person frail encourages unfair assumptions.

headwords.definition: the ability to move around independently
examples: A walking aid improved her mobility inside the home.
Limited mobility made public transport difficult.

headwords.definition: a short period of rest from a difficult duty
examples: Weekend respite allowed the caregiver to sleep and meet friends.
The center offers respite for families caring for disabled adults.

headwords.definition: the right to be treated as valuable and respected
examples: Helping with bathing requires attention to privacy and dignity.
The family protected their mother's dignity by including her in decisions.

headwords.definition: the period of grief after someone close dies
examples: Her workplace provided leave during family bereavement.
Different relatives responded to bereavement differently.

headwords.definition: money, property, or objects received when someone dies
examples: The siblings discussed the inheritance openly to avoid resentment.
A handwritten letter mattered more than the financial inheritance.

phrases.text: Care responsibilities should be shared as fairly as possible.
The person receiving care should remain involved in decisions.
Caregivers need rest before exhaustion becomes a crisis.
Practical support can protect both independence and dignity.
One sibling may contribute time while another contributes money.
Older age does not remove the right to privacy.
Families need honest conversations before care becomes urgent.
Grief does not follow the same schedule for every person.
Fairness may require different contributions rather than identical ones.

headwords.definition: a manageable relationship between paid work and family life
examples: Flexible hours improved her work–family balance after the baby was born.
A promotion may harm balance if travel increases greatly.

headwords.definition: care and supervision provided for children
examples: Reliable childcare allowed both parents to keep working.
The cost of childcare was almost equal to one salary.

headwords.definition: authorized time away from work after having or adopting a child
examples: Paid parental leave gave the family time to establish a routine.
Fathers taking leave can make caregiving more equal.

headwords.definition: a person whose income provides most household support
examples: The main breadwinner lost work, so the family used savings.
Treating fathers as automatic breadwinners limits choices.

headwords.definition: a person whose main work is managing a home and family
examples: The homemaker handled budgeting, meals, and care for two relatives.
Unpaid homemakers need financial security and recognition.

headwords.definition: work arrangements allowing choice over hours or location
examples: Flexible working helped him attend his mother's appointments.
Flexibility fails when staff must still answer all evening.

headwords.definition: a situation in which expected roles change
examples: Role reversal felt strange when the son managed his father's appointments.
Respectful care can make role reversal less humiliating.

headwords.definition: something valuable given up for another person or purpose
examples: The parents made a financial sacrifice for the child's education.
Family sacrifice should not always fall on the same person.

headwords.definition: something judged more important than competing demands
examples: Dinner together remained a priority during a busy month.
Her family priorities changed after becoming a caregiver.

phrases.text: Flexible work helps only when the workload remains reasonable.
Care responsibilities affect careers as well as private life.
Paid leave gives families time to adjust without losing income.
Unpaid household work has real economic value.
The family needs both income and time.
One person's career should not automatically take priority.
Roles can change after illness, retirement, or parenthood.
A sacrifice is easier to accept when it is recognized and shared.
Balance may look different at different stages of life.
Affordable childcare expands genuine choice for parents.
Family-friendly policies should be usable without career penalties.
